paragraphs: Of Freedom and Attention to Public Affairs

When a democratic state turns into an absolute monarchy, the activity that used to be directed at both public and private affairs is suddenly concentrated on private affairs alone. The immediate result, for a time, is great physical prosperity. But this impulse soon slackens, and the amount of productive industry is held back. I do not know whether a single trading or manufacturing people can be named, from the Tyrians down to the Florentines and the English, that was not also a free people. There is therefore a close bond and a necessary relation between these two elements, freedom and productive industry. This proposition is generally true of all nations, but especially of democratic nations. I have already shown that men who live in ages of equality constantly need to form associations in order to obtain the things they want. I have also shown how greatly political freedom improves and spreads the art of association. In these ages, then, freedom is especially favorable to the production of wealth. It is not hard to see that despotism is especially hostile to the same result. The nature of despotic power in democratic ages is not to be fierce or cruel, but petty and meddling. Despotism of this kind, though it does not trample on humanity, is directly opposed to the spirit of commerce and the pursuits of industry.

So men of democratic ages need to be free in order to get more easily the physical enjoyments they are always longing for. It sometimes happens, however, that the excessive taste they acquire for these same enjoyments hands them over to the first master who appears. The passion for worldly welfare then defeats itself and, without their noticing, pushes the object of their desires farther away.

There is, indeed, a most dangerous passage in the history of a democratic people. Among such a people the taste for physical gratifications may grow faster than education and experience of free institutions. Then the time will come when men are carried away and lose all self-restraint at the sight of the new possessions they are about to seize. In their intense and exclusive anxiety to make a fortune, they lose sight of the close connection between each person’s private fortune and the prosperity of all. It is not necessary to use force against such a people in order to strip them of the rights they enjoy. They willingly loosen their own hold. Carrying out political duties seems to them a troublesome annoyance that distracts them from their occupations and business. If they are required to elect representatives, to support the government by personal service, or to meet on public business, they have no time. They cannot waste their precious time on useless engagements. Such idle pastimes, they feel, are unsuited to serious men busy with the more important interests of life. These people think they are following the principle of self-interest, but their idea of that principle is a very crude one. To look after what they call their business, they neglect their chief business, which is to remain their own masters.

The citizens who work do not care to attend to public business, and the class that might have devoted its leisure to these duties has ceased to exist. The place of government is therefore, as it were, left empty. If at that critical moment some able and ambitious man seizes supreme power, he will find the road to every kind of usurpation open before him. If he looks after the material prosperity of the country for some time, nothing more will be asked of him. Above all, he must guarantee public tranquillity. Men possessed by the passion for physical gratification generally discover that the turmoil of freedom disturbs their well-being before they discover how freedom itself helps to promote it. If the slightest rumor of public commotion intrudes on the petty pleasures of private life, they are roused and alarmed by it. The fear of anarchy haunts them constantly, and they are always ready to throw away their freedom at the first disturbance.

I readily admit that public tranquillity is a great good. But at the same time I cannot forget that all nations have been enslaved by being kept in good order. This does not mean, certainly, that nations should despise public tranquillity. But that condition ought not to be enough for them. A nation that asks nothing of its government except the maintenance of order is already a slave at heart, the slave of its own well-being, waiting only for the hand that will bind it. In such a nation the despotism of a faction is no less to be feared than the despotism of an individual. When the bulk of the community is absorbed in private concerns, the smallest parties need not despair of gaining the upper hand in public affairs. At such times it is not rare to see on the great stage of the world, as we see in our theaters, a multitude represented by a few actors. They alone speak in the name of an absent or inattentive crowd. They alone are in action while everyone else stands still. They regulate everything by their own whim. They change the laws and tyrannize at will over the customs of the country. Then men are astonished to see into how few weak and worthless hands a great people can fall.

Up to now the Americans have fortunately escaped all the dangers I have just pointed out, and in this respect they truly deserve admiration. Perhaps there is no country in the world where fewer idle men are to be found than in America, or where all who work are more eager to promote their own welfare. But if the Americans’ passion for physical gratifications is violent, at least it is not indiscriminate. Reason, though unable to restrain it, still directs its course. An American attends to his private concerns as if he were alone in the world, and the next minute he gives himself up to the common good as if he had forgotten them. At one moment he seems driven by the most selfish greed, at another by the most lively patriotism. The human heart cannot be divided in this way. The inhabitants of the United States show, by turns, so strong and so similar a passion for their own welfare and for their freedom that it may be supposed these passions are united and mingled somewhere in their character. And indeed the Americans believe their freedom to be the best instrument and surest safeguard of their welfare. They are attached to the one because of the other. They by no means think that they are not called on to take part in the public good. On the contrary, they believe that their chief business is to secure for themselves a government that will allow them to acquire the things they want, and will not bar them from the peaceful enjoyment of the possessions they have acquired.
